==Problem 10== A box contains five cards, numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. Three cards are selected randomly without replacement from the box. What is the probability that 4 is the largest value selected? \textbf{(A) }\frac{1}{10}\qquad\textbf{(B) }\frac{1}{5}\qquad\textbf{(C) }\frac{3}{10}\qquad\textbf{(D) }\frac{2}{5}\qquad\textbf{(E) }\frac{1}{2} ==Solution 1 (combinational)== There are \binom{5}{3} possible groups of cards that can be selected. If 4 is the largest card selected, then the other two cards must be either 1, 2, or 3, for a total \binom{3}{2} groups of cards. Then, the probability is just {\frac{{\dbinom{3}{2}}}{{\dbinom{5}{3}}}} = \boxed{{\textbf{(C) }} {\frac{3}{10}}}. ==Solution 2 (regular probability)== P (no 5)= \frac{4}{5} * \frac{3}{4} * \frac{2}{3} = \frac{2}{5}. This is the fraction of total cases with no fives. p (no 4 and no 5)= \frac{3}{5} * \frac{2}{4} * \frac{1}{3} = \frac{6}{60} = \frac{1}{10}. This is the intersection of no fours and no fives. Subtract the fraction of no fours and no fives from that of no fives. \frac{2}{5} - \frac{1}{10} = \frac{3}{10} = \boxed{{\textbf{(C) }} {\frac{3}{10}}}. ==Solution 3 (Simple)== Pick any desirable situation. Let's say you first draw a 4, then a 3, then a 2. The probability of that is \frac{1}{5} * \frac{1}{4} * \frac{1}{3}, which is \frac{1}{60}. And for this case, it doesn't matter if you first draw a 3 or a 2. The probability of drawing a 4, a 3, and a 2 in any order is \frac{1}{60}. Next, list other desirable situations. You can draw a 4, 3, 1, or a 4,2,1, regardless of order. So, our desirable situations are 4,3,2, then 4,3,1, and lastly 4,2,1, regardless of order. Now, for each desirable situation, there are 3!=6 ways to arrange the numbers. That means that there are 6 ways to arrange 4,3,1, then 6 ways to arrange 4,2,1, and 6 ways to arrange 4,3,2. 6*3=18, which means, accounting for order, there are 18 desirable outcomes. The probability of each desirable outcome is \frac{1}{60}. Since there are 18 of them, the probability that 4 is the highest value selected is \frac{1}{60}*18, which equals \frac{18}{60}, which simplifies to the answer,\frac{3}{10}. This might be a lengthy explanation, but the idea behind it is pretty simple, and it doesn't take long for it to find the answer. Wish you luck on the AMC8! ~Evžen D. ==Solution 4 (Complementary Counting)== First we have to find the probability that we choose a 5. One of the three numbers is 5 and the other two have to be chosen from the set \{1,2,3,4\} so the number of sets with 5 as the largest number is \binom{4}{2}=6. The number of ways to choose a set of three from \{1,2,3,4,5\} is \binom{5}{3}=10, so that means that the probability that 4 is the highest number in the set is 10/10-6/10=4/10 right... nope! This is wrong because one of these sets that don't have 5 as the largest value also doesn't have 4 as it's largest value! We have over counted! So, we find the number of ways where 4 isn't in the set either. There is only one possibility because \binom{3}{3}=1. This means that there are only three ways to have a set with 4 as the largest value, so we find the probability to be \boxed{{\textbf{(C) }} {\frac{3}{10}}}. ~Shriyans.Chowdhury ==Solution 5 (List & Count)== Step 1: List every possible group of 3 cards. Since there are only 5 cards, list every possible set of 3 numbers:
1, 2, 3
1, 2, 4
1, 2, 5
1, 3, 4
1, 3, 5
1, 4, 5
2, 3, 4
2, 3, 5
2, 4, 5
3, 4, 5
Step 2: Find the groups where 4 is the biggest number. 1, 2, 4 ✓
1, 3, 4 ✓
2, 3, 4 ✓
Step 3: Turn it into a probability. Probability just means: (number of groups that work) out of (total number of groups). So the probability is 3 out of 10, or 3/10. ==Video Solution (CREATIVE THINKING!!!)== https://youtu.be/P-K9AEAuhNY ~Education, the Study of Everything ==Video Solutions== *https://youtu.be/OOdK-nOzaII?t=1237 *https://youtu.be/M9kj4ztWbwo https://youtu.be/FN9qkU62a9U ~savannahsolver *https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F935tcVcXvY ~davidxxxx ==See Also:== {{AMC8 box|year=2017|num-b=9|num-a=11}} {{MAA Notice}} [[Category:Introductory Probability Problems]] [[Category:Introductory Combinatorics Problems]]
